title: Force constant of a helical spring
objective: To plot a graph between load and extension for a helical spring.
To verify Hooke's law within the elastic limit.
To find the force constant k of the spring from the slope.

theory.statement: Within the elastic limit the extension x produced in a spring is directly proportional to the applied load F. This is Hooke's law, F = kx, where k is the force constant of the spring — the force needed to produce unit extension.
theory.derivationNote: A graph of load F (in newton) against extension x (in metre) is a straight line through the origin whose slope is k in N·m⁻¹. Beyond the elastic limit the material yields, the graph bends and the spring no longer returns to its natural length.
keyEquations: k = F/x = slope of the F-x graph
F = m·g with m in kg and g = 9.79 m·s⁻²

apparatus.name: Helical spring
apparatus.why: The specimen whose force constant is measured

apparatus.name: Rigid support and clamp
apparatus.why: Holds the spring vertically without yielding

apparatus.name: Slotted weights
apparatus.why: Applies a known, gradually increasing load

apparatus.name: Vertical metre scale
apparatus.why: Reads the pointer position before and after loading

apparatus.name: Pointer
apparatus.spec: fine tip attached to the lower end
apparatus.why: Marks the position of the spring's free end against the scale

procedure.text: Suspend the spring vertically from the rigid support and attach the pointer and hanger.
With no load on the hanger, note the pointer reading on the vertical scale. This is the zero-load position.
Add a 50 g slotted weight, wait for the spring to come to rest, and read the new pointer position.
Find the extension as the difference between the loaded and unloaded readings. Record it.
Repeat, adding 50 g at a time, for at least five loads, staying within the elastic limit.
Unload in the same steps and note the readings again to check for elastic after-effect.
Plot load in newton on the y-axis against extension in metre on the x-axis and draw the best-fit line.
Compute the slope of the line; this is the force constant k in N·m⁻¹.

steps: Convert each load to newton: F = (m/1000) × 9.79
Slope of the F-x graph = ΔF/Δx

expectedResult.statement: The load-extension graph is a straight line through the origin, verifying Hooke's law. The slope gives the force constant of the given helical spring.

safety: Do not overload the spring beyond its elastic limit — it will be permanently deformed.
Stand clear of the hanging weights; a slipping weight can fall on the feet.
Add and remove weights gently so the spring does not oscillate violently.
Check that the clamp and stand are stable before loading.
sourcesOfError: Parallax error while reading the pointer against the vertical scale.
Taking a reading before the spring has come to rest.
Elastic after-effect: the spring takes time to return to its original length after unloading.
The weight of the spring itself and of the hanger, which is not accounted for.
Loading beyond the elastic limit without noticing.

viva.question: State Hooke's law.
viva.expectedConcept: Within the elastic limit, stress is directly proportional to strain; for a spring, the extension is directly proportional to the applied force, F = kx.
viva.commonMisconception: Omitting the phrase 'within the elastic limit'.

viva.question: What is the force constant of a spring and what is its SI unit?
viva.expectedConcept: The force required to produce unit extension; SI unit newton per metre (N·m⁻¹).
viva.commonMisconception: Giving the unit as N/cm or as newton.

viva.question: What does the slope of the load-extension graph represent?
viva.expectedConcept: The slope of the load (N) versus extension (m) graph is the force constant k of the spring.
viva.commonMisconception: Taking the reciprocal of the slope as k.

viva.question: What is the elastic limit?
viva.expectedConcept: The maximum stress up to which a body regains its original shape and size completely on removal of the deforming force.
viva.commonMisconception: Confusing it with the breaking point.

viva.question: Two springs have force constants 10 N/m and 40 N/m. Which is stiffer and why?
viva.expectedConcept: The 40 N/m spring, because a larger force is needed for the same extension; its load-extension graph is steeper.
viva.commonMisconception: Thinking a larger k means the spring stretches more.

viva.question: Why should the load be increased in small, equal steps?
viva.expectedConcept: To obtain several evenly spread points for the graph and to detect the exact point at which the line begins to bend at the elastic limit.
viva.answerLogic: Graph quality and detection of yielding.
viva.commonMisconception: Saying only that it is 'more accurate'.

viva.question: What happens if you exceed the elastic limit?
viva.expectedConcept: The spring is permanently deformed; the graph curves away from the straight line and the spring does not return to its original length when unloaded.
viva.commonMisconception: Believing the spring simply breaks immediately.

viva.question: If the same spring is cut into two equal halves, what is the force constant of each half?
viva.expectedConcept: Each half has twice the force constant of the original spring, because for the same force each half extends only half as much.

preLab.question: The SI unit of the force constant of a spring is:
preLab.feedback: k = F/x, so the unit is newton per metre.

preLab.question: A load of 100 g exerts a force of about:
Hooke's law holds only:
preLab.feedback: Beyond the elastic limit the proportionality between load and extension breaks down.

duringLab.question: Record at least five readings within the elastic limit.
Note the zero-load pointer reading before adding any weight.

postLab.question: State the force constant of the steel spring you obtained (N·m⁻¹).
postLab.feedback: The steel spring supplied has a force constant of about 24.5 N·m⁻¹.

postLab.question: Your load-extension graph is a straight line through the origin. This shows that:
options: The spring has exceeded its elastic limit
postLab.feedback: A straight line through the origin means direct proportionality, which is Hooke's law.

postLab.question: If your graph bends at the top, the most likely reason is:
postLab.feedback: Bending at high loads is the signature of yielding beyond the elastic limit.

scientificValidation.formula: F = kx; k = slope of load-extension graph
assumptions: Spring obeys Hooke's law below the elastic limit
Mass of the spring is negligible
Readings taken after the spring comes to rest
scientificValidation.validRange: Load 0-450 g for the steel spring; 0-320 g brass; 0-600 g stiff
scientificValidation.unitSystem: SI; load entered in gram, extension read in cm, both converted for the graph
edgeCases: Zero load must give zero extension
Load beyond the elastic limit adds a super-linear term
Load under 20 g gives an extension below the least count
expectedBehaviour: Extension directly proportional to load while elastic
Stiffer spring gives a steeper graph and a larger k
k recovered within 1% from simulated readings
